item.title: N.Y.C. Council Members Call for More Restrictions on Tech in Schools
item.description:
Senior members of the City Council on Tuesday called for the broad removal of technology in New York City’s public schools and expressed alarm over the widespread use of digital devices in classrooms.

This push comes two weeks after the city’s Department of Education announced some restrictions on tech in schools that the council members believed could be tougher. They want to strictly limit tools for the youngest students, including the elimination of devices like laptops or tablets before middle school. They called for a return to handwritten assessments and paper books.

Eric Dinowitz, the chair of the Council’s Committee on Education, also urged school leaders to get rid of video-game-style instructional apps. Parents have complained that they are addictive and that some apps prompt their children to sign up for monthly subscriptions to unlock more features.

“This is really damaging, much in the same way as social media,” Mr. Dinowitz said at a joint hearing of the education committee and the Council oversight and investigations committee.

Officials painted a dire picture of technology, which they said has become so ingrained in classroom instruction since the pandemic that it has hooked students on devices starting in elementary school, stunting their development of social skills, critical thinking and problem solving.

The reliance on digital devices most likely played a part in recent sharp declines in reading test scores, they said, and collided with many parents’ efforts to curb screen time at home.

“Parents, teachers and advocates are rightly concerned that the use of ed-tech products in our schools has become obsessive and is distracting students from having to learn,” said Shekar Krishnan, a City Council member from Queens. “We must do more.”

The demands for stricter limitations were the latest push back to the intrusion of technology in young children’s lives in New York City, which is home to the nation’s largest school system. In the city and across the country, parents have increasingly united around concerns that school districts had hastily embraced digital devices without evidence that they were beneficial and are now doing the same with artificial intelligence.

At the hearing, Department of Education officials said they shared the concerns about unfettered, unnecessary use of technology and about its potentially negative effect on student learning.

Danielle Giunta, the first deputy chancellor at the Department of Education, said school leaders were committed to removing tools that did not help students, including recently disabling access to YouTube on school-issued devices. She also said that some video-game-style apps would be removed under the school system’s new tech policy.

She acknowledged that technology had rapidly spread in the classroom after students returned from remote learning during the pandemic.

“We thought we were sending our children back and that our laptops would close,” Ms. Giunta said. “We do need to look at it, slow it down and study it better.”

If enacted, the council members’ proposed limitations would go beyond the sweeping restrictions that the Department of Education recently unveiled for A.I. and screen time. The department’s policies are among the most restrictive of any school district in the country.

Starting this school year, students are barred from using A.I. tools before high school or using individual screens before third grade. Older students in elementary school can use individual devices for up to 30 minutes per day, and the time limit increases to 45 minutes for middle schoolers.

High schoolers have more freedom to use tablets or laptops. They also can use certain A.I. tools for a short period of time every day. Nearly 40 instructional tools with A.I. features that students used last year will be disabled. So-called companion chatbots, which provide emotional and mental support, are banned in all grades.

There are some exceptions to the A.I. limitations. They do not apply to some student tests, or services to help students with disabilities, some of whom use A.I. tools to communicate.

Until now, principals and teachers in the city’s roughly 1,600 schools largely set their own rules on screens and A.I. The new rules will last at least a year and then could be extended or amended, school officials said.
